# The Harness {#sec-the-harness}

The harness is the runtime around the model that turns each suggested next
action into bounded, observable work. It assembles model input, records
progress, dispatches tools, waits for approval, enforces limits, and gives a
person reliable ways to pause or stop a run.

An agent run divides responsibility among four roles. The model proposes the
next action. The harness sequences those proposals into steps and records each
one durably. Policy and identity systems decide whether an action is
authorized, and the harness enforces their decision. Tools and the external
systems behind them carry out the effects; the harness coordinates attempts at
an effect, and whether a repeated attempt takes effect only once depends on the
receiving system. Keeping these roles separate prevents a convenient agent loop
from being mistaken for a transaction manager or a security principal.

## The runtime contract

At its smallest, a harness repeats three operations: ask a model, execute an
accepted tool call, and append the result. A production runtime also has to
answer questions the loop leaves open:

| Concern | Contract the harness must expose |
|---|---|
| Identity | Which user, tenant, agent definition, and run produced this step? |
| State | What was durably accepted, and which work is still outstanding? |
| Authority | Which policy and approval authorize this exact action now? |
| Effects | Was an external operation committed, rejected, duplicated, or left with an unknown outcome? |
| Control | Where do pause, steer, cancel, kill, and fork take effect? |
| Limits | What time, cost, calls, bytes, mutations, and concurrency remain? |
| Recovery | What may be replayed, and what must first be reconciled? |

A useful formalization is a versioned transition function:

$$
(S_{t+1}, C_t) = \delta_v(S_t, e_t).
$$

Here, `e_t` is an accepted event: a user command, model result, tool result,
approval decision, timer, or recovery observation. `C_t` is the set of commands
the transition emits. The state `S_t = (r, h, w, m, p, k, b, q)` contains:

- `r`: run identity, status, and agent-definition version;
- `h`: the durable history head;
- `w`: the workspace or sandbox reference;
- `m`: the application-memory view and its version;
- `p`: the principal, policy snapshot, and approval records;
- `k`: the admitted tool-catalog version;
- `b`: remaining and reserved budgets; and
- `q`: outstanding work, attempts, leases, and unresolved effects.

The transition function is called the reducer because it folds each accepted
event into the run state. The reducer is versioned because recovery must
interpret old history with the same semantics that produced it. It should be
deterministic over accepted events even when model and tool outputs are not.
Four invariants follow:

1. A terminal run emits no new commands.
2. Every effect command records its actor, scope, approval, stable step ID,
   attempt number, idempotency key, and input fingerprint.
3. Budgets never increase except through an explicit, authorized grant.
4. One completion is accepted for an attempt lineage; late or duplicate results
   are retained as evidence but cannot silently advance state twice.

This event history is the source for restart and audit. A checkpoint is an
optimization derived from that history, and the history remains authoritative.
It records a verified history position plus the versions, pending operation
IDs, deadlines, workspace references, and known effect outcomes needed to
continue.

## Runs are explicit state machines

The states below are deliberately explicit. A client that receives `paused` or
`waiting for approval` should not have to infer that condition from missing
tokens on a stream. Likewise, `needs reconciliation` is a visible state of its
own, which tells the client to reconcile an unknown outcome before any retry.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `created` | Identity, definition, and initial budgets have been recorded. |
| `ready` | Admission succeeded; no child operation is active. |
| `running` | The reducer is processing an accepted event. |
| `waiting_model` | Waiting for model; the UI can display “waiting for model.” |
| `waiting_tool` | Waiting for tool; the exact call and deadline are visible. |
| `waiting_approval` | Waiting for approval before dispatching an effect. |
| `paused` | No new work is scheduled; resumable state remains durable. |
| `cancelling` | Cancellation was accepted and active children are being stopped. |
| `completed` / `failed` | Terminal success or terminal known failure. |
| `needs_reconciliation` | An external outcome is unknown or inconsistent. |

```{dot}
//| label: fig-harness-state-machine
//| fig-cap: "A harness state machine. The waiting and paused states share one box because each returns to running. A tool call whose outcome is unknown moves the run to needs reconciliation, and it returns to running only after the outcome is resolved. Waits and reconciliation are visible states, not gaps in an output stream."
digraph {
    bgcolor="transparent";
    rankdir=TB;
    nodesep=0.24;
    ranksep=0.32;
    node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#374151", fillcolor="#f1ece1"];
    edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

    C [label="created"];
    R [label="ready"];
    X [label="running"];
    W [shape=Mrecord, style="filled", label="{<m>waiting\nfor model|<t>waiting\nfor tool|<a>waiting\nfor approval|<p>paused}"];
    K [label="canceling"];
    Q [label="needs\nreconciliation", fillcolor="#f2d6a2"];
    D [label="completed\nor failed", fillcolor="#cfe8cf"];

    C -> R -> X;
    X -> W -> X;
    X -> K -> D;
    W:t -> Q;
    Q -> X [label="resolved"];
    X -> D;
}
```

The transition journal must be committed before a command is delivered. That
ordering prevents a worker crash from erasing the reason a tool was called.
It leaves one uncertainty window open: an external system may commit a write
just before the worker crashes and records its receipt. Recovery must therefore
establish what happened to an effect before it replays the step that issued it.

## Pin definitions; adapt protocols explicitly

Instance lifetime and definition versioning are independent choices. A shared
runner can resolve immutable configuration per run; a freshly allocated runner
can still load an unversioned prompt. Pin each run to an agent-definition
version containing its instructions, model route, tool schemas, policy
references, and harness reducer version. Record that version in every
checkpoint. A rollout policy then routes *new* runs to a canary or stable
definition and states whether existing runs remain pinned, migrate at a safe
boundary, or stop.

Without per-run resolution, the prompt and model binding are deploy-time constants
shared by every session, and a regression reaches every session until the rollback
completes. OpenAI's sycophantic GPT-4o update shows the timescale: it rolled out on
April 25, 2025, rollback began on April 28, and the full revert took about 24 hours
[@openai2025sycophancyexpanded]. A definition resolved per run confines a regression
to the canary slice while pinned runs keep the stable version. The price is a
resolution step on every run, a consistency requirement across replicas, and one more
version to read in every incident.

Provider protocols differ in features and semantics. A compatibility adapter
should publish a feature matrix for tool calls, structured output, streaming,
cancellation, usage data, continuation identifiers, and error semantics. When a
feature cannot be represented, fail explicitly or declare the downgrade. Do
not silently interpret “request accepted” as feature parity. Pin adapter and
provider versions alongside the agent definition so an evaluation or incident
can reproduce the actual path.

A coding harness is usually built against one provider's dialect, so pairing it
with another provider's model goes through a translation gateway. The gateway maps
each request through an intermediate representation, and because the dialects are
not isomorphic the mapping can drop fields such as reasoning settings, cache
directives, or tool options. A gateway that reports each dropped field to the caller
lets the loss be tested; one that forwards what it can and discards the rest changes
behavior silently.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Claude Code speaks the Anthropic Messages API, and a gateway in front of it must
expose Messages, Bedrock InvokeModel, or Vertex rawPredict and forward the
`anthropic-version` and `anthropic-beta` headers [@anthropic2026gatewayprotocol].
Codex supports only the Responses wire protocol for a model provider
[@openai2026codexconfig]. Open-weight serving engines expose OpenAI-compatible
endpoints, and vLLM also serves the Anthropic Messages API [@vllm2026repo].
:::

## Control verbs have different meanings

Pause, resume, steer, cancel, kill, and fork are separate capabilities, not
strength levels of one interrupt:

- **Pause** stops scheduling at a documented safe point. Active calls either
  finish, are canceled, or remain listed as unresolved.
- **Resume** continues a paused state under compatible definition and policy
  versions. If those changed, migration is an explicit transition.
- **Steer** appends a user command to durable history. The contract says whether
  it applies before the next model call or after current work finishes.
- **Cancel** records `cancel_requested`, rejects new work, and fans the request
  out to active children. Cooperative code must observe it; an RPC cancellation
  alone does not interrupt arbitrary server code [@grpc2024cancellation].
- **Kill** forcefully terminates harness-owned execution, such as a process
  group or sandbox. It is an escalation path, not a rollback mechanism.
- **Fork** creates a new run namespace from a checkpoint, with isolated mutable
  state and a new idempotency scope. External effects committed before the fork
  point apply to both the original run and the fork.

Cancellation has two useful milestones. It is **acknowledged** when the request
is durable and no new commands will be scheduled. It is **quiescent** when all
harness-owned children have stopped or been marked unresolved. Remote work can
continue after the harness stops waiting, and cancellation cannot undo a
committed external effect. The runtime must reconcile, compensate, or ask an
operator what to do with an unknown outcome. Temporal makes the same practical
distinction between graceful cancellation and forceful termination, and notes
that a remote activity needs cooperative heartbeats to receive cancellation
[@temporal2026cancellation].

An approval is another interruption, but it carries an integrity requirement.
Show the approver the exact tool, target, arguments or diff, acting identity,
expected effect, and cost. Bind the decision to a unique call ID and immutable
payload hash; make it scoped, expiring, and single-use. Re-run authorization and
input guardrails immediately before dispatch. If the payload or relevant policy
changed while paused, require a new decision. Serializable pause-and-resume
approval flows demonstrate the mechanism, including approvals raised by nested
agents [@openai2026hitl]. They do not replace execution authorization.

## Durable work, duplicate delivery, and external effects

A resumable harness persists durable history independently of prompt context.
Workers consume commands from a queue, claim them with a bounded lease, and
write results against a stable step ID and attempt number. A lease limits
concurrent ownership; it does not prove the previous owner stopped. For a
correctness-critical resource, attach a monotonically increasing fencing token
and require every write path to reject stale tokens [@kleppmann2016distributed].
Without receiver-side validation, the token is only metadata.

```{figure}
//| figure: lease-fencing
//| label: fig-harness-lease-fencing
//| fig-cap: "One lease, two workers, and the receiver of their writes, on a time axis. Worker A holds the lease with fencing token 33, renews it every 2 s (ticks under the lease bar), and pauses just before its write. When the pause outlasts the lease TTL, the lease expires, worker B takes it with token 34 and writes, and A then resumes and writes as if it still held the lease. Only a receiver that checks tokens refuses that stale write; with no token, or a token nothing checks, it replaces B's result. A stale write that reaches the receiver before any write with a newer token is accepted in every mode. Timings are illustrative."
```

Scheduling uses the same model. Give each occurrence a stable identity such as
`(schedule_id, scheduled_at)` and claim it through a durable unique record.
Duplicate delivery and execution are still possible. Kubernetes documents that
even a single-completion Job may start the same program twice
[@kubernetes2026jobs]. A scheduler lease prevents overlap while it remains
valid, and duplicate effects still have to be handled at the receiver.

Whether an occurrence continues one persistent session or starts a fresh one is a
separate choice. A persistent session lets a monitoring agent compare against last
week's baseline, but its history grows without bound and makes context projection
mandatory. A fresh session per occurrence is correct when occurrences are
independent. A persistent session for a stateless job stores history nothing reads,
and a fresh session for a job that needs history discards it every time.

Effect safety depends on the receiver:

| Operation | Retry rule |
|---|---|
| Read-only or proven idempotent | Bounded exponential backoff with jitter. |
| Receiver-keyed write | Reuse the same idempotency key; reject a different input fingerprint for that key. |
| Write with unknown outcome | Query status and reconcile before retry; compensate or require review if status is unavailable. |
| Authentication, authorization, validation, or business-rule failure | Normally non-retryable; surface it. |

Persist the error class, next-attempt time, absolute deadline, and retry budget
so a restart cannot reset the policy. Automatic retries are useful because
operations can fail transiently, and an activity may therefore execute more than
once and should be designed accordingly [@temporal2026retry].

Locks also belong at the resource they protect. A session lock serializes one
conversation; it cannot protect a branch, customer account, or deployment
touched by another run. Use resource-level concurrency through conditional
writes, database constraints, protected branches, merge queues, or a lock keyed
to the actual resource. A Git worktree separates local files; pushes from
different worktrees to the same remote still need one of these resource-level
controls. Such collisions are routine: a dataset of more than 142,000 pull requests
opened by five coding agents reports a merge-conflict rate of 27.67 percent
[@ogenrwot2026agenticflict].

Database locks carry a pooling hazard. A PostgreSQL session-level advisory lock is
held by the server connection until it is released or the connection closes, and a
session that already holds it acquires it again immediately
[@postgresql2026advisory]. PgBouncer's transaction pooling hands a server connection
to a different client after each transaction and does not support session-level
advisory locks [@pgbouncer2026features]: a `pg_advisory_lock` taken through it stays
on a pooled connection, the unlock may run on another, and a later client handed the
same connection acquires the lock as if it were free. A transaction-scoped
`pg_advisory_xact_lock`, or a dedicated session-pooled connection, keeps the lock
with the work that holds it.

## A tool is a typed, authorized effect boundary

Beyond a name and a JSON input schema, the harness needs a tool contract that
can drive admission, approval, execution, retry, and result handling:

```text
ToolSpec {
  name, input_schema, output_schema, side_effect_class,
  auth_scopes, approval_rule, timeout, retry_class,
  idempotency, max_output_bytes, sandbox_profile
}

ToolResult {
  status, payload | artifact_ref, receipt,
  error_class, observed_at
}
```

Four gates must remain separate:

1. **Catalog admission** decides whether a tool definition and implementation
   are trusted enough to register.
2. **Per-turn exposure** selects the smallest relevant candidate set for the
   model. Retrieval improves selection, and permission still comes only from
   execution authorization.
3. **Execution authorization** checks the current principal, tenant, action,
   resource, arguments, policy, and bound approval immediately before dispatch.
4. **Result handling** validates structure, caps inline size, stores large
   outputs as artifacts, records receipts, and treats returned text as
   untrusted data.

Tool names, descriptions, schemas, and results are all untrusted model input.
Signing and review reduce tool poisoning (a tool definition that carries
instructions aimed at the model), while authorization still applies to
every concrete call, including calls made by a child agent. The Model Context
Protocol (MCP), a standard interface between agent hosts and tool servers,
similarly defines tools with input and optional output schemas, asks clients to
validate results, and recommends keeping a human able to deny sensitive
invocations [@mcp2025tools]. Its authorization guidance also forbids passing
arbitrary tokens through to downstream servers and requires tokens to be bound
to their intended resource [@mcp2025security; @campbell2020resource].

No universal tool-count threshold determines when a flat catalog fails. Measure
selection quality with the actual model, schemas, and task distribution. When
the catalog grows, retrieval, namespacing, or model-driven discovery can reduce
per-turn exposure, but each adds a failure mode: missing the required tool,
surfacing a dangerous irrelevant tool, or spending additional calls on
discovery.

The three mechanisms differ in who selects. Tool retrieval indexes names,
descriptions, and argument descriptions and loads the best matches for each turn.
Namespacing exposes a subset per phase, such as read-only tools while diagnosing
and write tools while fixing, which requires the harness to track the phase.
Model-driven discovery gives the model a search tool and lets it ask, so discovery
quality depends on the model. Tool definitions also sit near the start of the
prompt, where a provider's prompt cache keys on the exact prefix; a scheme that
rewrites the tool list each turn invalidates the cache from that point on, while one
that appends discovered definitions later in the conversation keeps the cached
prefix intact.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Anthropic's API provides a tool search tool. Definitions marked `defer_loading` stay
out of the context; the model searches names, descriptions, and argument
descriptions by regular expression or BM25, and matching tools are expanded inline
without changing the cached prompt prefix. A request can defer up to 10,000 tools,
and the documentation reports that the model's tool selection degrades once more
than 30 to 50 tools are loaded [@anthropic2026toolsearch].
:::

## Stateful tools: separate three kinds of state

“Stateful tool” hides three different responsibilities:

- **Connection state** includes transport sessions, negotiated capabilities,
  cursors, and backpressure.
- **Durable resource state** lives in the external system: a file, ticket,
  transaction, or remote job.
- **Model-visible state** is an explicit handle or summary passed in later
  turns.

Recovery should reconnect, rediscover capabilities, and resume from a cursor or
explicit handle when the protocol supports it. Otherwise it starts a new
connection without pretending that durable resource state vanished.

Connection state is also what limits horizontal scaling. Holding connections in
memory per replica, keyed by `(session_id, server_url)`, works on one replica. When
a replica holding $N$ sessions, each connected to $M$ servers, fails, recovery opens
$N \times M$ connections at once against the surviving replicas, each renegotiating
capabilities and losing its cursor. The mitigations follow from that mechanism:
session affinity keeps a connection on one replica, reconnect backoff with jitter
spreads the reconnections over time, and resumable streams make each reconnection
cheap. MCP's transports moved along the same path. Streamable HTTP replaced the
earlier HTTP with Server-Sent Events transport and lets a client resume a stream
from its last event ID within an `Mcp-Session-Id` session [@mcp2025transports]. The
transport working group then set out to remove protocol-level sessions
[@mcp2025transport], and the 2026-07-28 specification drops the initialization
handshake and the protocol session, so any request can reach any replica and state
that spans calls travels as an explicit handle the model passes back as an ordinary
argument [@mcp2026rc; @mcp2026release]. Authorization changed across the same
dated versions [@mcp2025changelog], so a harness pins the protocol version and
designs to its declared guarantees, without assuming that every connection is a
durable session.

## Context is a projection of history

The canonical history contains accepted commands, model and tool results,
approval decisions, receipts, source links, and unresolved obligations. The
working context is a lossy projection of that history:

$$
K_t = P(H_{\le t}, B_t, T_t),
$$

where `P` selects material from canonical history `H`, within context budget
`B`, for current task state `T`. Prompt context, durable execution history, and
the personalization memory of @sec-personalization are different stores.

Compaction can summarize old turns. Masking can replace bulky observations with
typed placeholders. Large outputs can become an artifact reference. Retrieval
can restore evidence for the next decision. Every option loses something, so
the projection should report what it omitted and preserve links back to source
events. Compacting working context does not delete canonical evidence. In
particular, it must preserve active constraints, pending approvals, incomplete
plans, effect receipts, failures, and the provenance of any summary.

Longer context does not remove this design problem. Controlled studies find
that performance can degrade with input length even when retrieval is correct
[@du2025context], while simple observation masking can rival more elaborate
summarization in software-agent settings [@lindenbauer2025complexity]. The
choice is empirical and task-specific.

## A sandbox has several independent walls

“Runs in a container” is not an isolation contract. Specify each dimension:

| Dimension | Minimum question |
|---|---|
| Process | Can code signal, inspect, or escape into host or sibling processes? |
| Filesystem | Which paths are mounted, writable, persistent, and shared? |
| Network | Is egress default-deny, and which destinations and protocols are allowed? |
| Credentials | Are long-lived secrets absent and capabilities issued only for a checked action? |
| Resource limits | What CPU, memory, PIDs, disk, output, and network ceilings apply? |
| Lifetime | What survives pause, restart, cancellation, kill, expiry, and deletion? |

A worktree is not a security boundary. It reduces file collisions between
coding runs and leaves the kernel, processes, network, host credentials, and
any container-runtime socket shared. Untrusted execution needs a
sandbox appropriate to the threat model, such as a hardened container,
user-space kernel, or microVM, plus non-root execution, restricted mounts,
dropped privileges, system-call policy, and default-deny egress
[@nist2017containers].

For correctness between cooperating agents, the worktree is the stronger of the
cheap options. In a study of asynchronous multi-agent software engineering, agents
in separate worktrees scored 59.1 percent on Commit0-Lite, against 56.1 percent for
agents instructed to edit only their own files in one shared workspace and 53.1
percent for a single agent. On PaperBench the instruction-only arrangement scored
55.5 percent, below the single agent's 57.2 percent, while worktrees reached 63.3
percent [@geng2026asynchronous]. An instruction to stay out of another agent's
files holds only while the model complies; a separate worktree holds regardless.

Do not mount long-lived secrets. A broker can issue short-lived, narrowly
scoped, audience- and resource-bound credentials after validating the exact
action. The broker must also redact logs and support rotation and revocation.
These controls reduce credential theft and blast radius; whether an authorized
action is safe remains a question for policy and approval. Killing a local
sandbox does not revoke an external effect already committed under its
credential.

## Budgets and admission must compose

The harness keeps limits as a ledger of reservations. Before starting a model
or tool call, reserve its worst allowed consumption; after completion,
reconcile the actual usage and release the remainder. Reject work that cannot
be reserved. Enforce independent ceilings for wall-clock and idle time, model
calls, input and output tokens, money, tool calls, external mutations, bytes,
child runs, concurrent operations, and sandbox resources. The wall-clock ceiling
holds even when token accounting lags, because the harness measures elapsed time
itself; one user report describes a Claude Code session whose plan-and-execute loop
and recursive hooks consumed about 1.67 billion tokens in five hours
[@claudecode2025tokens].

The order of checking and charging decides whether a ceiling holds under
concurrency. The cell below runs the same workload under two ledgers. One checks
that the run is under budget, launches up to $c$ calls, and charges each call when
it returns; the other reserves each call's declared worst cost before launch and
releases the unused part on completion. The first overshoots by up to $c$ times the
worst call, because every call in flight passed the check before any of them was
charged; the cell asserts that bound and asserts that the reserving ledger never
exceeds the ceiling and stops less than one worst-case call short of it. Raise
`worst` to see the price of reservation: a looser declared maximum leaves more
budget unused at the end.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
B, worst, trials = 1000.0, 8.0, 2000  # budget ceiling, declared worst cost of one call, runs per point
widths = np.array([1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32])  # calls the harness lets run concurrently

def final_spend(c, reserve):
    """Spend at the end of each run; calls launch in waves of up to c and are charged on completion."""
    spent, open_ = np.zeros(trials), np.ones(trials, bool)
    while open_.any():
        if reserve:  # admit a call only if its worst case still fits under the ceiling
            n = np.minimum(c, np.floor((B - spent) / worst))
        else:        # check the ledger, charge after the call returns
            n = np.where(spent < B, c, 0)
        n = np.where(open_, n, 0)
        cost = rng.uniform(1, worst, (trials, c)) * (np.arange(c) < n[:, None])
        spent += cost.sum(axis=1)
        open_ = n > 0
    return spent

check = [final_spend(c, reserve=False) for c in widths]
held = [final_spend(c, reserve=True) for c in widths]
assert all((s <= B).all() and (B - s < worst).all() for s in held)
assert all((s - B < c * worst).all() for s, c in zip(check, widths))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.8))
ax.plot(widths, [s.max() / B for s in check], "o-", color="#c0392b", label="check, then charge: worst run")
ax.plot(widths, [s.mean() / B for s in check], "o--", color="#c0392b", alpha=0.5, label="check, then charge: mean")
ax.plot(widths, (B + widths * worst) / B, ":", color="0.3", label="bound: ceiling + c × worst call")
ax.plot(widths, [s.max() / B for s in held], "s-", color="#2471a3", label="reserve worst case: worst run")
ax.axhline(1, color="0.6", lw=1)
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2); ax.set_xticks(widths, [str(w) for w in widths])
ax.set_xlabel("concurrent calls c"); ax.set_ylabel("final spend / budget ceiling")
ax.set_title("Charging after the call overshoots; reserving stays under the ceiling")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```
::::

A child receives a sub-budget carved from its parent's remaining budget. Parent
and child reservations therefore remain under the same monotone ceiling. Store
absolute deadlines so a restart cannot grant more wall-clock time, and
propagate the remaining deadline downstream. A local timeout only bounds how
long the harness waits; remote work or billing may continue and must be
canceled or reconciled separately.

Admission combines identity and policy checks with atomic quota or capacity
reservation. A preflight capacity query is advisory because capacity can change
before scheduling. Bounded queues, per-tenant concurrency, priority and
fairness, startup deadlines, backpressure, and explicit `pending` conditions
make scarcity visible. Kubernetes resource quotas constrain aggregate namespace
consumption, while a Pod remains Pending when its request cannot be scheduled
[@kubernetes2026quotas; @kubernetes2026resources].

Circuit breakers solve a different problem. They protect callers from a failing
dependency with closed, open, and probe states. They do not replace run budgets
and should not classify “exit code zero” as task success. Use structured result
status, receipts, postcondition checks, and explicit goal verification.

## Evaluate the harness as a system

A harness change is itself an experimental treatment, because it can move the
measured result. Compare it under a fixed model, task set, tool implementations,
policy, sampling configuration, and resource envelope. Record the exact agent
definition, harness and adapter versions, effective request, tool schemas,
sandbox profile, and environment. Report task quality alongside the mechanisms intended to protect it:

- task success and invalid-tool-call rate;
- tool-selection precision and recall;
- approval-bypass rate and unauthorized-effect rate;
- cancellation acknowledgment latency and quiescence latency;
- post-cancel effect count and duplicate-effect rate;
- recovery divergence and unresolved-effect rate;
- context-critical-loss rate after compaction;
- isolation escape rate; and
- added latency and added cost against a minimal baseline.

Then inject failures at the boundaries: crash between external commit and
journal receipt; deliver a command twice; expire a lease while a worker is
paused; revoke authorization after approval; hang a subprocess; fill the queue;
poison a tool description; compact just before a critical constraint; and fork
after an effect. A clean happy-path trace does not exercise the contract.

The same dependence carries over to published benchmark scores whenever the
benchmark is interactive. Over a long episode the harness decides what carries
from one model call to the next, which is the context projection described
earlier in this chapter, so one model can score differently on the same tasks
under two harnesses. ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of turn-based game environments
whose rules are not stated, shows the effect directly. ARC Prize's standard
harness carries forward only the notes the model chooses to keep. Its
provider-adapter harness also preserves the provider's opaque reasoning state
between requests, reasoning from earlier calls that the harness keeps but
cannot read, and compacts long conversations. After the two harnesses gave one
model different results, ARC Prize began reporting
both, each labeled [@arcprize2026astra]; @sec-capability-horizon gives the
figures. A score from an interactive benchmark therefore names its harness and
adapter version, and a comparison across providers states whether it held one
harness fixed or let each provider use its own adapter.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint arrow
Scores attributed to an agent are joint properties of the model, harness,
tools, and environment. Benchmark infrastructure can leak answers or expose a
grader that an agent learns to exploit: an audit of ten agent benchmarks found 219
flaws and built exploits that reach near-perfect scores on most of them without
solving the intended tasks [@rdi2025trustworthy]. A held-out answer key protects
against memorized answers and does nothing against an agent that reads the grader.
Therefore
@sec-benchmarks and @sec-evaluating-agents must report and hold the harness
version fixed when comparing models. A provider configuration file is useful,
but the effective serialized request and observed response are the stronger
reproduction artifacts when adapters insert defaults or omit unsupported
fields.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What remains contested
Two questions remain open. First, no context-projection strategy reliably knows
which detail a future step will need; compaction, masking, retrieval, and larger
windows trade different errors. On SWE-bench Verified, masking old observations
matched LLM summarization's solve rate at the lowest cost in four of five
configurations, and summarization lengthened trajectories by 13 to 15 percent: the
summaries appear to hide the failure signals that would tell an agent to stop
[@lindenbauer2025complexity]. Learned compression guidelines report lower peak token
use with higher task success on long-horizon benchmarks [@acon2025context], while
longer windows degrade with input length even when retrieval is perfect
[@du2025context; @hong2025contextrot]. The runtime can trigger compaction and reload
an externalized plan at the right moment; whether the summary keeps what the next
step needs depends on the model that writes and reads it. Second, a portable harness can normalize common
operations but cannot manufacture provider capabilities or identical error and
cancellation semantics. Both are product choices that a generic “agent” API
should state explicitly, and both should be measured.
:::

## Operational contract checklist

Before trusting a harness with a long run, verify that it can answer:

- Which immutable definition and reducer version own this run?
- What event was accepted last, and what work or effect is unresolved?
- What exact payload and policy authorize the next side effect?
- When is cancellation acknowledged, and when is owned work quiescent?
- Which retry classes are safe, and who enforces idempotency?
- What remains in each parent and child budget?
- Which process, filesystem, network, credential, resource, and lifetime walls
  contain execution?
- Can recovery and fault-injection tests demonstrate these claims?

A harness that can answer these questions makes an agent operable: each run can
be inspected, interrupted, recovered, and bounded. The next chapter,
@sec-computer-use, puts this contract under more pressure: a graphical
interface creates longer action chains, weaker state observations, more
latency, and side effects that are harder to identify before execution.
